primary_cause: COVID-driven demand shock to ride-sharing/travel exposure
secondary_factors: Growth-stock de-risking and high-beta tech selloff
store_description: Uber fell harder than the broad market because investors were suddenly discounting weaker ride volume in travel-heavy and dense urban markets even before the company formally withdrew guidance later in the spring. The most plausible explanation is a rapid repricing of mobility demand risk as the outbreak globalized.

primary_cause: Bernie Sanders won Nevada caucuses Feb 22. Medicare for All risk repricing
secondary_factors: General COVID market selloff
store_description: UNH's drop was too large to explain by the broad tape alone and lined up with a sector-specific healthcare-insurer selloff tied to Sanders' front-runner status. Contemporary coverage described UnitedHealth as having one of its worst days in years as investors repriced the risk of aggressive healthcare reform.

primary_cause: COVID supply-chain and global shipping disruption. Had canceled 22 China flights
secondary_factors: Weaker air-cargo and international-commerce expectations
store_description: UPS was exposed both to China-related freight disruption already underway and to the market's new fear that the problem was becoming global rather than China-contained. The stock's decline fits a logistics-demand and supply-chain risk repricing rather than any single fresh UPS announcement.

primary_cause: COVID risk to cross-border payment volumes and travel spending
secondary_factors: Broad selloff in travel- and consumer-exposed financials
store_description: Visa's business model was especially sensitive to international travel and cross-border card activity so the rapid spread of COVID outside China immediately raised concern that high-margin transaction growth would slow. No cleaner company-specific catalyst found in the 3-day window.

primary_cause: Oil-demand shock from COVID. OPEC cut 2020 demand view Feb 12 (-200k bpd)
secondary_factors: Pressure on whole energy complex and fears of further OPEC action
store_description: Exxon traded down with crude as the market moved from China demand problem to global demand problem. With oil already down roughly 15% year-to-date by OPEC's Feb. 12 report and then falling again on Feb. 24 the stock's decline is best explained by commodity and demand exposure.

primary_cause: Broad tech/software selloff tied to COVID
secondary_factors: Valuation compression in large-cap software
store_description: Oracle's decline was almost exactly in line with the Nasdaq's drop and there is no strong evidence of a company-specific catalyst in the window. This looks like a macro-led move in large-cap software.

primary_cause: Macro COVID repricing of ad-sensitive mega-cap tech
secondary_factors: Momentum unwind in big tech
store_description: Alphabet fell roughly in line with other large-cap tech as the market digested a possible global growth shock. No evidence that antitrust or a company filing was the main driver in this exact Feb. 21-24 window.

primary_cause: COVID-driven industrial recession fears
secondary_factors: Global supply-chain disruption and cyclical de-risking
store_description: Emerson is tied to industrial automation and process markets so the stock sold off with cyclicals as the outbreak threatened manufacturing output and customer spending. No stronger company-specific catalyst found.

primary_cause: COVID supply-chain and auto-demand fears. China operations at low production rates
secondary_factors: Concern about parts availability and weaker global vehicle demand
store_description: GM's drop fits the market's reassessment of automakers as China-linked production and demand risk spread beyond China. This looks like a sector exposure move rather than a single GM-specific headline.

primary_cause: Macro COVID repricing of ad-sensitive mega-cap tech
secondary_factors: Momentum unwinding in FAANG/mega-cap growth
store_description: GOOG and GOOGL moved together because the market was selling broad Alphabet exposure not reacting to a class-specific event. The available evidence points to macro growth fears overwhelming everything else.

primary_cause: Feb 17 Apple warned it would miss March-quarter revenue guidance ($63-67B) due to COVID
secondary_factors: Broad COVID market selloff and renewed concern over China supply chains
store_description: This was one of the clearest stock-specific names on the list. Apple had already told investors it would miss March-quarter guidance because of slower production normalization and weaker demand in China and Feb. 24's market panic amplified that preexisting company-specific negative.

primary_cause: Broad COVID market selloff
secondary_factors: Mild healthcare equipment/China supply-chain concern
store_description: Abbott did not show the kind of outlier move that would strongly imply a company-specific catalyst. This looks like a market-led decline with modest sector spillover rather than Abbott-specific bad news.

primary_cause: COVID-driven concern over enterprise spending
secondary_factors: Broad tech/services de-risking
store_description: Accenture's business is tied to large corporate budgets and transformation work so the stock was vulnerable as investors suddenly repriced global growth and CIO spending assumptions. No more direct company-specific trigger found.

primary_cause: Valuation compression in software amid COVID shock
secondary_factors: General Nasdaq/momentum selloff
store_description: Adobe's decline was somewhat steeper than the S&P 500 but broadly consistent with the Nasdaq-led drawdown in premium software names. Not much evidence for a discrete Adobe catalyst.

primary_cause: Semiconductor supply-chain fear amplified by Apple's Feb 17 warning and COVID spread
secondary_factors: Broader semiconductor de-risking
store_description: Even without an AMAT-specific filing the evidence points to a sector read-through. Apple's warning highlighted the real operating impact of the outbreak and semi-equipment names were vulnerable to both factory disruption and order delays.

primary_cause: Semiconductor COVID/supply-chain shock. High-beta momentum unwind
secondary_factors: Apple's miss warning added credibility to supply chain fears
store_description: AMD's nearly 8% drop strongly suggests a sector-plus-beta move rather than a new company-specific disclosure. Investors were punishing semiconductor names exposed to hardware supply chains and cyclical demand uncertainty.

primary_cause: Broad COVID panic hitting mega-cap growth/consumer exposure
secondary_factors: Near-term logistics and supply-chain worries. Before stay-at-home narrative
store_description: On Feb. 24 the market was still pricing the immediate shock not the later e-commerce upside narrative. Amazon therefore sold off with the rest of big tech as investors focused on disruption risk rather than potential demand substitution toward online retail.

primary_cause: Travel-and-T&E spending risk from COVID
secondary_factors: Broader financials selloff and consumer-spending fears
store_description: AmEx's business mix was uniquely vulnerable to a sudden freeze in travel and corporate entertainment spend. With airlines and travel demand already under pressure and the outbreak spreading outside China the stock's 5% drop looks like a direct read-through from collapsing travel expectations.

primary_cause: COVID-driven airline/travel-demand shock layered onto existing 737 MAX fragility
secondary_factors: Investor concern about cash burn and aircraft demand
store_description: Boeing did not need a new company-specific headline to fall on Feb. 24 because it was one of the most vulnerable names to any sudden deterioration in airline economics. The market was effectively stacking a pandemic-related aviation shock on top of an already damaged Boeing thesis.

primary_cause: Falling yields and recession fears from COVID. Rates market drove it
secondary_factors: Broad risk-off selling in financials
store_description: For BAC the key transmission mechanism was the rates market. Investors rushed into safe-haven Treasuries yields fell and bank earnings expectations compressed. The move looks far more like a macro/rates shock than a BAC-specific news event.
